evidence_notes.research_design: Structured critical review of more than 20 primary studies published from 2015 to 2025. It classifies six software-engineering-agent architectures and compares reported benchmark resolution rates, estimated per-issue costs, and a synthesized six-category failure taxonomy.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: This is a cross-study comparison, not a matched experiment. The performance table mixes systems, base models, years, and SWE-bench variants; cost values are published or estimated. A relatively close reported comparison is GPT-4o Agentless 1.0 versus GPT-4o SWE-search on SWE-bench Lite, but the review does not rerun either system under a shared harness. The Agentless model swap also demonstrates that model and architecture effects can be confounded.
headline_results: Role specialization and cross-agent validation can provide redundant checking, but flawed upstream specifications can be faithfully propagated and same-base-model agents can reinforce correlated errors.

The reported table gives Agentless 1.0 a 27.3% SWE-bench Lite resolution rate at about $0.34 per issue versus 23.0% at about $4.00 for GPT-4o SWE-search; the review therefore rejects architectural complexity as a reliable performance predictor.

Within Agentless, changing the reported base model from GPT-4o to Claude 3.5 Sonnet raises SWE-bench Lite resolution from 27.3% to 40.7%, which the authors use to argue that base-model quality is a major performance driver.
Reported costs range from $0.34 to more than $10 per issue among systems with similar resolution rates, making cost efficiency a first-class production constraint.
The review's bounded claim is task-dependent: adaptive agents may help on genuinely long-horizon work, whereas structured pipelines are favored for well-defined localization-and-repair tasks.
No surveyed architecture fully addresses hallucination, context overflow, test overfitting, over-engineering, inter-agent correlated errors, and security-boundary violations together.
limitations: The review aggregates heterogeneous published results rather than executing a matched same-task, same-model, same-tool comparison.

Dominant benchmarks overrepresent open-source Python repositories and may contain pretraining or temporal leakage; enterprise code, proprietary frameworks, security-sensitive review, multi-session refactoring, and stakeholder coordination are underrepresented.
Leaderboard results are often closed-source, single-run, and reported without confidence intervals, seeds, inference parameters, or training-data provenance.
Resolution rate can reward test-overfit patches and omit semantic correctness, regression behavior, security, and test-coverage quality.
TheAgentCompany adds professional tasks but has only 175 tasks, which the authors consider insufficient for statistically reliable characterization.
future_work: Combine LLM patch generation with model checking, formal verification, or differential testing for semantic guarantees.
Create adversarial and ecologically valid benchmarks targeting specific failure modes, multiple languages, security, and human-agent workflows.
Develop uncertainty-aware agents, cross-session memory, and security policies integrated into architectures rather than added after deployment.
Disclose seeds, inference parameters, and training-data provenance and evaluate repeated runs with confidence intervals.
Develop task-complexity criteria based on issue length, relevant-file count, underspecification, tool-selection accuracy, and self-correction rate to decide when agentic complexity is warranted.
combinable_methods: Use deterministic fault localization, multi-patch sampling and ranking, and syntax filtering as a low-cost default pipeline.
Add hierarchical repository-to-file-to-function retrieval or AST-based navigation only where cross-file context requires it.
Ground generation with retrieved code and use semantically independent validators or diverse base models to reduce correlated errors.
Pair automated tests with semantic, differential, formal, and non-regression checks.
Enforce containerization and explicit permission controls for tools and file-system access.
Route tasks to simple pipelines or adaptive agents according to measured task complexity rather than defaulting to maximum orchestration.

quotes.text: Multi-agent frameworks overcome single -agent lim itations through role specialization and cross -agent validation. MetaGPT made the software engineering roles (product manager, architect, engineer, tester) into structured agent interactions through standardized documents. This process mitigates hallucina tion due to redundant verification. However, it also has the downside of coordination overhead.
quotes.use: States the proposed specialization mechanism and its immediate coordination cost.

quotes.text: When multiple agents are instantiated from one and the same underlying LLM, their outputs will not differ too much. Such problems must be taken into account in any critical analysis of multi -agent systems. When many agents make the same mistake, we call it a correlated error. We think that debate will correct these. But it actually reinforces them.
quotes.use: Qualifies same-model debate and identifies correlated-error reinforcement.

quotes.text: Cost per resolved issue has become an important secondary metric in practice. The measured range between systems from $0.34 (Agentless) to $10+ (some multi -agent configura tions) differs by more than an order of magnitude for systems achieving similar resolution rates, a difference notably not highlighted in benchmark leaderboard presentations.
quotes.use: Documents the order-of-magnitude production-cost spread hidden by accuracy-only leaderboards.

quotes.text: The optimum degree of architectural complexity is probably task -dependent: complex agents can afford genuine advantages on long -horizon tasks requiring adaptive decision -making, while structured pipelines outperform for the well -defined localiz ation-and- repair tasks that constitute most current benchmarks.
quotes.use: Bounds when agentic complexity may be justified instead of treating it as universally beneficial.

evidence_notes.research_design: Controlled comparison of Supervisor tool-calling, Hierarchical, and deterministic Custom orchestration for a shared Builder-Validator-Fixer React pipeline. The study uses 75 user stories and paired Figma designs from four projects, six generator-judge model pairings drawn from GPT, Gemini, and Claude, and reports 450 experimental instances plus a manual audit of 180 judge ratings.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Architectures receive the same datasets, standardized tools, specialized-agent sequence, prompts, token accounting, and model families. Generator and judge are always different models to reduce self-preference, and prompts and API versions are fixed. This isolates coordination strategy among three multi-agent implementations, but there is no direct single-agent generation baseline, so the study cannot establish that the multi-agent pipeline itself beats one agent.
headline_results: Architecture changes quality by only about 3-5 percentage points but changes generator token use substantially; the deterministic Custom workflow has the best reported cost-quality balance.

Custom averages 1.40 million generator tokens versus 2.47 million for Hierarchical and 3.10 million for Supervisor, while full functional coverage is 53.3%, 51.3%, and 49.5%, respectively, and full visual fidelity is 58.1%, 53.0%, and 56.8%.
Prompt/context duplication, not additional code generation, explains the architecture-level token difference; prompt tokens make up 60-70% of usage.
Judge agents average 5.9 times the generator token use and are the dominant evaluation cost, so validation can erase gains from cheaper generation.

Across all configurations, full functional coverage is 54.1% and full visual fidelity is 57.9%; counting partial matches raises them to 76.9% and 84.9%, but complex domain-specific interactions remain difficult.

A maximum of two validation-repair cycles, refusal retries, JSX cleanup, and file scaffolding repair many low-level failures without full regeneration; 42 of 144 GPT attempts recover after retry and 13 remain unrecovered.
Gemini-judge configurations suffer systematic visual-evaluation failures, demonstrating that the evaluation layer itself can be a production reliability fault.
limitations: There is no single-agent baseline; all compared conditions use the same specialized Builder-Validator-Fixer pipeline.
The dataset contains only four open-source Figma/React projects and 75 user stories, limiting generalization to proprietary, larger, or enterprise systems.
The study evaluates front-end React generation only and excludes backends, authentication, dynamic data binding, and more complex state management.

Categorical LLM-as-judge labels may miss fine-grained behavior and visual quality; manual agreement ranges from 0.55 to 0.90, and two Gemini-judge configurations produce no visual scores because of systematic evaluation failure.
Findings depend on specific checkpoints and prompts; the paper notes prompt sensitivity and possible behavior changes after model updates.
Even with partial matches, the authors state that production-grade quality still requires human refinement and better handling of complex interactions.
future_work: Evaluate the workflow on larger proprietary and full-stack applications with authentication, backend data, and complex stateful interactions.
Develop lower-cost evaluation workflows because judge inference dominates total token consumption.
Improve handling of non-standard and domain-specific interactions that produced the lowest functional and visual coverage.
Retain human refinement for production-grade acceptance and validate judge outputs against broader human review.
combinable_methods: Use a deterministic finite-state Build-Validate-Fix graph when task dependencies are known.
Separate visual scaffolding from behavioral enrichment and map stories to only the relevant components to constrain context.
Cap validation-repair loops to prevent oscillation and require programmatic checks for blank renders, missing files, and compilation errors.
Retry detected refusals under a fixed policy, then sanitize code fences, pre-code and post-code text, missing exports, paths, and project files with deterministic repair tools.
Use a different model for judgment than generation and manually audit a sample of judge decisions.
Track tokens separately for generators and judges so architecture and evaluation costs remain visible.

quotes.text: Each round of fixes is re-evaluated by the Val- idator, with a maximum of two validation–repair cycles to prevent oscillation and ensure stable convergence.
quotes.use: Provides a concrete bounded-loop stability mechanism.

quotes.text: The token efficiency differences arose from how much context each architecture needed to duplicate and re-read, not from differences in reasoning or generation complexity.
quotes.use: Identifies duplicated context as the cause of orchestration overhead.

quotes.text: Judges are the domi- nant cost drivers, consuming roughly 3.3× (Supervisor), 8.1× (Hi- erarchical), and 7.7× (Custom) more tokens than Generators (Ta- ble 3). Averaged across architectures, this is about 5.9× more overall.
quotes.use: Quantifies evaluation cost as the production bottleneck.

quotes.text: The Hierarchical architecture consumed 26–126% more tokens than the Custom architecture but achieved lower functional and visual accuracy (51.3% vs. 53.3%; 53.0% vs. 58.1%).
quotes.use: Shows that extra coordination hierarchy did not improve quality under the controlled architecture comparison.

quotes.text: These results indicate that most failures stem from low-level formatting inconsistencies rather than conceptual reasoning errors, and that lightweight recovery and cleanup methods effectively stabilize the generation pipeline.
quotes.use: Supports deterministic post-processing and retry as low-cost reliability measures.

evidence_notes.research_design: Exploratory controlled case study of two role-specialized agents, Designer and Programmer, on one open-ended Fibonacci-game task in C. Twelve pairings from seven open-source LLM families run under a deterministic Python controller with fixed minimal role prompts, temperature 0.5, cumulative history, a 10,000-iteration cap, and two repeated runs. Analysis combines thematic coding, BLEU/ROUGE, word counts, manual correctness checks, and GCC 11.4 compilation.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The task, role prompts, controller, turn-taking, termination rules, token cap, and decoding temperature are held fixed across pairs, and every pair is run twice. Model identity, model size, reasoning specialization, and symmetric versus asymmetric pairing vary together; the 12 pairings are not a full factorial design. There is no single-agent baseline, and repeated-run details are not reported separately because the authors observed no substantial differences.
headline_results: Only DeepSeek-R1 paired with itself begins with a correct solution and sustains it to the end; three other pairs start correctly but diverge after 3, 21, or 69 iterations, and the remaining eight never reach the required solution.
No pair starts off-task and later discovers the correct answer, so prolonged conversation provides no observed recovery benefit in this task and can destroy an already correct result.

Strong role alignment or compilation success does not establish task correctness: Qwen3:Qwen3 and LLaMA 3.2:LLaMA 3.2 compile 100% of extracted C programs but never initiate the required correct solution.
The sole convergent DeepSeek-R1 pair exhibits semantic echoing and many no-code turns, showing that convergence, interaction quality, role separation, and compiler success are distinct dimensions.
Despite a C-only Programmer prompt, generated code is 61% C, 37.9% C++, and 1.1% Python, evidencing instruction and platform drift.
Pair compatibility and interaction dynamics matter more than model size or lexical overlap in this case study; reasoning-model participation alone does not ensure progress.
limitations: The study uses one open-ended Fibonacci-game task, so correctness and convergence depend on task-specific evaluation criteria and may not generalize to other tasks, prompts, or languages.
Only 12 selected open-source model pairings are tested; proprietary models, future versions, dynamic roles, and larger teams are outside scope.
BLEU and ROUGE measure lexical overlap and may not capture nuanced reasoning or non-literal correctness.
The experiment has no single-agent baseline and does not isolate model family, parameter count, reasoning design, or pair symmetry independently.
The very high 10,000-turn ceiling exposes stagnation but is unlike a cost-bounded production workflow; token cost and latency are not reported.
Compilation analysis considers only C snippets found in conversations and labels instruction-only turns as no code, so compilation rate is not equivalent to end-to-end success.
future_work: Replicate on more complex tasks, programming languages, model populations, prompts, and richer agent roles.
Add tool integration and study whether compiler feedback changes divergence and recovery behavior.
Disentangle whether DeepSeek-R1 convergence is caused by reasoning design or model scale.
Calibrate explicit convergence and termination policies using repetition, topic adherence, role stability, and correctness signals.
combinable_methods: Use deterministic turn-taking and preserve complete trace logs for role and topic analysis.
Validate candidate code with a compiler and behavioral tests rather than semantic alignment scores alone.
Stop or checkpoint immediately after verified correctness instead of allowing unconstrained post-solution dialogue.
Monitor repetition, topic drift, role reversal, language drift, and no-code turns as runtime health signals.
Trigger model switching, prompt revision, human intervention, or fallback execution when monitored traces stagnate.
Select agent pairs empirically for the target role and task rather than assuming heterogeneous or reasoning-model pairs are compatible.

quotes.text: Together, these findings suggest that simply allowing agents to interact is insufficient and a deeper empirical understand- ing of how coordination unfolds over time is necessary to build reliable autonomous SE systems.
quotes.use: Rejects unstructured interaction as a sufficient coordination mechanism.

quotes.text: Overall, these results indicate that interaction behavior in multi-agent LLM systems is strongly model-dependent and prone to episodic breakdowns that are not captured by mean-level statistics alone.
quotes.use: Supports pair-specific and trace-level reliability evaluation.

quotes.text: A good compilation success rate i.e., effectiveness could be accompanied with poor role alignment, again convergence can come along with a lot of semantic echoing.
quotes.use: Separates syntactic success, role quality, and correct convergence.

quotes.text: In other words, we observed no cases where agents began off-task and only later discovered the correct solution. This suggests that once a correct solution emerges, it tends to be preserved for a bounded number of iterations (≤ 69 in our study), while later recovery is unlikely.
quotes.use: Motivates early stopping after verified correctness and shows lack of late recovery.

quotes.text: In practice, monitoring the interaction trace can help detect early signs of failure, such as repetition, drift, or role instability before time and compute are wasted on unproductive exchanges.
quotes.use: Provides a production-oriented trace-monitoring method.

evidence_notes.reason: No full text retrieved; do not infer from abstract.

evidence_notes.research_design: Ablation-based controlled experiment on 100 ClassEval Python class-generation tasks. Three model backends, GPT-4o-Mini, DeepSeek-Chat, and Claude-3.5-Haiku, each run a RawPrompt baseline and four role-specialized Waterfall configurations comprising Requirement, Design, Implementation, and Testing agents. The 1,500 generated samples are evaluated with class/function Pass@1, SonarQube issue density, runtime exceptions, and manual root-cause classification.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Each model is compared against its own direct-prompt baseline on the same ClassEval tasks and official tests. The four workflow variants remove Requirement, Design, or Testing one at a time while retaining Implementation, which isolates stage contributions better than cross-system leaderboard comparisons. All models use temperature 0.8. Only one first sample is scored, minor syntax errors are manually corrected before rerunning tests, and generated tests make the Testing-stage treatment partly model-dependent.
headline_results: Role-specialized Waterfall processing is not uniformly better than one direct agent: full-workflow class Pass@1 falls from 0.35 to 0.21 for GPT-4o-Mini and from 0.46 to 0.32 for DeepSeek-Chat, while Claude-3.5-Haiku rises from 0.21 to 0.22.
Workflow effects are model-dependent; the Claude variant without Design reaches the best Claude class Pass@1 of 0.29, whereas RawPrompt remains best for the other two models.

Waterfall stages reduce missing-code and consistency issues and can improve maintainability, but generally increase reliability and adaptability issues and shift failures toward semantic logic, return contracts, and overrestrictive validation.
Runtime-error counts increase by 10-53% over RawPrompt across Waterfall configurations; ValueError, AssertionError, and TypeError dominate while some low-level errors decline.

Testing has the largest stage effect. Omitting it often produces the poorest correctness and highest error counts, but including it can add reasoning and validation faults; Requirement and Design show comparatively limited effects.
SonarQube reports no Security or Responsibility issues in any condition, so the experiment supplies no discriminating security result despite measuring those categories.
limitations: The evidence is limited to 100 Python ClassEval tasks and may not generalize to repositories, other languages, or full development projects.
Pass@1 scores only one temperature-0.8 sample, so stochastic variance may affect model and workflow differences.
Generated Testing-agent tests may not cover all behavior, and function-level Pass@1 can misrepresent classes with interdependent methods.
Manual failure classification is partly subjective, and the experiment manually repairs minor syntax punctuation before rerunning tests.
The study reports no token, latency, or monetary-cost comparison, so cleaner code cannot be assessed against orchestration expense.
No security defects are observed, but ClassEval is not described as a security or adversarial benchmark.
future_work: Build adaptive pipelines that select stages according to model and task rather than imposing the complete Waterfall workflow.
Add cross-stage consistency checks and prioritize benchmark specifications when generated stage artifacts conflict.
Define clearer contracts and report both functional correctness and maintainability or quality outcomes.
Improve failure diagnosis while reducing subjectivity in root-cause classification.
combinable_methods: Retain requirement clarification and test planning but make design and validation conditional rather than rigid.
Constrain validators to explicit requirements to avoid adding unsupported input restrictions.
Check method signatures, return types and formats, and edge cases at every handoff.
Use official behavioral tests alongside static maintainability and reliability measures.
Apply cross-stage consistency checks before implementation and cap Developer repair at a small fixed number of cycles.
Choose stage composition per model using ablation evidence instead of treating role decomposition as universally beneficial.

quotes.text: Waterfall-style, role-based agents can improve code structure and maintainability by encouraging clearer design and validation. But this extra structure often adds checks or con- straints not required by the specification, which can lower execution success andPass@1.
quotes.use: States the central quality-versus-correctness mechanism behind over-structured specialization.

quotes.text: Overall runtime errors increase by 10–53% under Waterfall workflows compared to RawPrompt.
quotes.use: Quantifies the reliability regression against the direct-prompt baseline.

quotes.text: Waterfall workflows reduce structural errors such asMissing Codebut increase reasoning and validation issues such asSemantic FailureandReturn Mismatch.
quotes.use: Shows that role decomposition changes rather than simply removes failure modes.

quotes.text: We isolated all failing classes from the 1,500 RQ2 sam- ples (100 ClassEval tasks×3 models×5 workflows) and manu- ally inspected each to determine the root cause.
quotes.use: Documents the scale and manual basis of the root-cause evidence.

quotes.text: We mainly use Pass@1 to measure functional correctness. Because it evaluates only the first generated solution, it can be affected by randomness and may not fully capture model ability.
quotes.use: Captures the primary conclusion-validity limit of the matched comparison.

evidence_notes.research_design: Controlled mixed-method requirements-elicitation study across mental-health journaling, personal finance, and fitness. It compares one-shot single-model, iterative single-model, two-model, and three-model simulated focus groups with human focus groups and Emotional Goal Modeling. The main design includes 24 AI and six human sessions; primary-domain same-model controls add two seeds each. Twenty-four independent source-blinded raters evaluate requirements, with coded dialog mechanisms, equal-effort downsampling, mixed models, and pooled meta-analysis.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: C0 versus C1 isolates iteration; C1 versus C2/C3 adds model plurality while holding six personas, prompts, turn caps, and orchestration constant. C1-MV and C3-SM same-model controls in the primary domain partly separate multi-voice structure from provider capability. Creator models voice their own personas, session order is randomized, human-baseline order is counterbalanced, and requirement raters are blinded to source. The same-model controls have only two seeds and one domain, so provider and plurality effects remain partly confounded.
headline_results: Three-model plurality raises the pooled validated AI-only requirement share by 14.7 percentage points over the iterative single-model workflow, with a 95% confidence interval of 11.2 to 18.2 points.

Same-model controls estimate a 9.3-point difference-in-differences attributable to plurality structure rather than provider capability in the primary domain, although those controls are small and domain-specific.

Persona diversity, contradictions, productive-conflict density, empathy events, and conflict resolution all increase from C0 through C3; pooled productive-conflict density correlates with validated AI-only yield at Spearman rho 0.86.

C3 requirements are more innovative than EGM requirements, while EGM is clearer and more feasible and human focus groups better ground natural tone and social acceptability; no method dominates every quality dimension.

The supported use is early requirements divergence, not replacement of users: heterogeneous simulated voices broaden candidate requirements, structured EGM makes goals and trade-offs traceable, and human engagement validates context, trust, and acceptability.

C3 runs are capped at roughly 10^4 generated tokens and yield about 15-18 AI-only clusters with 8-10 validated, versus about 12-14 clusters and 4-5 validated for C1; monetary cost and downstream implementation success are not evaluated.
limitations: Same-model ablations use fewer seeds and only the primary domain, leaving residual confounding between plurality and provider capability.
Prompts, guardrails, and moderator challenge turns can shape disagreement and yield; provider drift and seed proxies limit exact reproducibility.
Validated share depends on human rating interpretation, relevance cutoffs, coding, embedding clusters, and cosine thresholds.
Only three consumer domains, six human participants per baseline/domain, and seven reflective interviews are studied, limiting transfer to other products, regulations, and organizations.
Provider/model diversity is not cultural diversity because training data and evaluation are predominantly English and Western.
Synthetic personas have no lived experience and must not replace affected users, especially for sensitive domains.
The study evaluates requirements novelty and perceived quality, not whether implementing those requirements improves software outcomes.
future_work: Test multilingual prompts, region-specific models, culturally diverse participants, and additional regulatory and product contexts.
Replicate same-model plurality controls with more seeds and across all domains.
Examine alternative prompts, moderation rules, validation thresholds, and clustering cutoffs.
Trace validated requirements through implementation and outcome evaluation rather than stopping at elicitation quality.
combinable_methods: Use heterogeneous models for divergent candidate generation, then EGM goal-to-requirement traces for structure and human focus groups for grounding.
Preserve creator-voice mapping so heterogeneous perspectives remain active during discussion.
Bound turns and tokens, detect role breaks, retry once, log prompts and model versions, and retain turn-to-requirement traceability.
Measure productive conflict and empathy rather than raw disagreement, and require conflict to produce a refined requirement within a bounded window.
Deduplicate candidates with embeddings followed by human adjudication and validate them with source-blinded independent raters.
Apply stereotype guardrails, privacy defaults, consent controls, transparency hooks, and human review before prioritizing sensitive requirements.

quotes.text: We do not claim that simulated focus groups replace affected users or human focus groups in sensitive domains. Instead, we position them as a fast, reproducible way to expand the space of candidate ERs early, which then must be vetted, contextualized, and prioritized with people.
quotes.use: Bounds the specialist simulation claim to augmentation rather than stakeholder replacement.

quotes.text: A random-effects meta-analysis pooled the C3– C1 difference at +14.7% (95% CI:[+11.2,+ 18.2]), confirming a robust plurality advantage (diamond in Fig. 5A).
quotes.use: Provides the pooled controlled effect of three-model versus iterative single-model elicitation.

quotes.text: At the session level, productive-conflict density strongly predicted the validated AI-only share.
quotes.use: Identifies productive rather than merely frequent disagreement as the proposed gain mechanism.

quotes.text: Plurality diverges and reframes familiar pains (e.g., guilt after lapses) into new design moves; EGM structures these moves via transparent goal→subgoal→requirement tracing, improving feasibility and clarity; human groups ground language, tone, and social accept- ability.
quotes.use: Defines the complementary diverge-structure-ground production workflow.

quotes.text: Provider plurality is not the same as cultural diversity: most models are trained on predominantly English and Western data, and our evaluation pool is limited; future work should incorporate multilingual prompts, region-specific models, and culturally diverse participants to test whether the same mechanisms hold.
quotes.use: Limits model heterogeneity as a proxy for real stakeholder diversity.

evidence_notes.research_design: Empirical taxonomy study of 998 GitHub issue reports from CrewAI and LangGraph between December 2023 and January 2026. From 2,773 collected open and closed issues, bug labels leave 1,010 and manual filtering leaves 998. Two annotators construct an initial taxonomy from 100 random issues and classify 15 root causes and seven symptoms across five lifecycle stages.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The authors scrape all open and closed issues to reduce sampling bias, require a maintainer or contributor bug label, manually exclude non-bugs, and use two independent annotators with consensus. CrewAI supplies a role-based collaborative architecture and LangGraph a graph/state orchestration architecture. This is not an exposure-normalized framework comparison and includes no single-agent versus multi-agent performance control, execution reproduction, or matched task workload.
headline_results: API Misuse accounts for 32.97% and API Incompatibility for 22.34% of reports, jointly 55.3%, while Documentation Desync adds 7.52%; execution semantics and changing contracts dominate framework reliability.
The Self-Action stage contains the largest concentration and symptom diversity, especially scheduling, tool invocation, graph execution, and state flow.
Across all issues, Functional Error accounts for 78.26%, Crash for 10.02%, and Build Failure for 6.71%; many systems keep running while state, planning, or tool coordination behaves incorrectly.

In Mutual Interaction, API Misuse represents 37.74% and Streaming Instability 15.09% of stage bugs; 92.45% of that stage's symptoms are Functional Errors affecting delegation and shared-state consistency.

Framework faults can propagate upward into agent applications and the LLM software supply chain, causing incorrect execution, resource misuse, and security risk independently of model reasoning quality.
limitations: Only CrewAI and LangGraph are studied, so other orchestration, tool, memory, and deployment frameworks may have different failure distributions.
The corpus is restricted to GitHub reports carrying a bug label; unreported, security-sensitive, silently tolerated, and mislabeled defects may be absent.
Taxonomy labels infer primary root causes from issue text and comments; disagreements are resolved by consensus, but no inter-rater statistic is reported.

Counts are not normalized by framework users, versions, releases, agent executions, or lifecycle-stage exposure, so they are prevalence within the curated report corpus rather than operational failure rates.
The study does not reproduce failures or measure severity, repair time, exploitability, downstream task accuracy, token cost, or single-agent versus multi-agent differences.
Filtering excludes documentation requests and infrastructure issues that do not involve framework logic, narrowing the represented production surface.
future_work: Develop lifecycle-aware testing and analysis that detects execution-semantic bugs before deployment.
Study state consistency, coordination, and resource-management bugs in multi-agent and long-running workflows.
Standardize APIs, dependency management, and runtime monitoring to reduce recurring systemic faults.
Extend empirical analysis to more frameworks and connect issue taxonomies to executable reproductions and repair evaluation.
combinable_methods: Test initialization, perception, self-action, mutual interaction, and evolution as distinct lifecycle stages.
Add API contract and compatibility tests around scheduling, tool invocation, message serialization, streaming, and graph execution.
Keep documentation synchronized with lifecycle semantics and executable API examples.
Pin and test dependency combinations and validate runtime configuration before agent execution.
Instrument state transitions, tool calls, delegation, streaming, and memory persistence with runtime monitoring.
Exercise shared-state consistency, concurrency, execution isolation, and long-running memory in integration tests.

quotes.text: When bugs arise in LLM agent frameworks, they can propagate to upper-layer systems and amplify their impact, leading to incorrect execution, resource misuse, and security risks.
quotes.use: Establishes framework bugs as a production and software-supply-chain risk.

quotes.text: From 998 issue reports, we identify 15 root cause cate- gories, with ‘API Misuse’ (32.97%) and ‘API Incompatibility’ (22.34%) accounting for over 55% of all cases. Most root causes concentrate in the ‘Self-Action’ stage, indicating that mechanisms related to execution semantics are the primary source of framework bugs.
quotes.use: Quantifies the dominant framework root causes and lifecycle stage.

quotes.text: The ‘Mutual Interaction’ stage features coordination failures, including ‘API Misuse’ (accounting for 37.74% of this stage) and ‘Streaming Instability’ (accounting for 15.09% of this stage), which disrupt delegation logic and shared state consistency.
quotes.use: Directly identifies coordination and shared-state failure mechanisms.

quotes.text: Future work can explore lifecycle-aware testing and analysis meth- ods to detect execution-semantic bugs early. As agent ecosystems evolve, research should address state-consistency, coordination, and resource-management bugs in multi-agent and long-running workflows. Finally, integrating our insights into framework de- sign, including standardized APIs, dependency management, and runtime monitoring, may help reduce systemic failures.
quotes.use: Provides the paper's production-readiness methods and research agenda.
